title: Quantum Advantage for Distributed Symmetry Breaking
abstract: We present a distributed quantum algorithm that $3$-colors cycles in $O(1)$ rounds, with high probability. It follows that all locally checkable labeling problems (LCLs) that have round complexity $O(\log^* n)$ in the classical LOCAL model can be solved in $O(1)$ rounds in the quantum-LOCAL model, with high probability; this includes problems such as maximal independent set and maximal matching in bounded-degree graphs. This presents the first natural examples of graph problems with an asymptotic distributed quantum advantage for the LOCAL model; all prior examples that separate LOCAL and quantum-LOCAL are artificial problems constructed merely for the sake of demonstrating quantum advantage.

bite.hook: We present the first natural graph problems with an asymptotic distributed quantum advantage for the LOCAL model.
tldr: They designed a distributed quantum algorithm that 3-colors cycles in O(1) rounds with high probability.
They proved that classical LCL problems taking O(log* n) rounds can be solved in O(1) rounds using a quantum-LOCAL model.
They demonstrated the first natural examples of graph problems showing asymptotic distributed quantum advantage.
bite.whyItMatters: Proving that quantum networks can solve complex network coordination problems exponentially faster than classical networks opens the door to fundamentally faster distributed computing.
bite.eli5: Imagine trying to paint a giant ring of houses so no two adjacent houses share a color, using walkie-talkies to talk only to your immediate neighbors. A quantum network can finish this game in a constant number of steps no matter how huge the neighborhood gets, whereas a regular network would take much longer as it scales up.

glossary.shortDef: A standard model in distributed computing where nodes communicate with neighbors in synchronous rounds.
glossary.eli5Def: A rulebook for studying how computers in a network solve problems by only talking to their direct neighbors.

glossary.shortDef: A set of vertices in a graph such that no two are connected and no more can be added.
glossary.eli5Def: Choosing the largest group of people in a room where nobody is friends with anyone else in the group.

glossary.shortDef: Graph problems whose correctness can be verified by checking a constant-radius neighborhood around each node.
glossary.eli5Def: A puzzle where you only need to look at your immediate neighbors to know if everyone followed the rules.
